concept.name: Long call butterfly
concept.definition: A long call butterfly is a three-strike, same-expiration spread built from calls only: long one call at a lower strike, short two calls at a middle strike, and long one call at a higher strike, with the middle strike equidistant from the wings. Entered for a small net debit, it reaches maximum value when the underlying finishes exactly at the middle strike.
concept.intuition: You are buying a target: a cheap bet that the stock will land near the middle strike at expiration, with the wings defining your worst case.
concept.mechanics: Net debit = (lower call + upper call) - 2 x middle call; the position is worth zero outside the wings and peaks at the wing width at the body strike. It is a combination of a bull call spread and a bear call spread sharing the short middle strike, and it is short volatility between the wings.
concept.formula: Value at expiration = max(0, min(S_T - K1, K3 - S_T)) when K2 - K1 = K3 - K2; max value = K2 - K1 at S_T = K2; max loss = net debit.
concept.failure_modes: The profit zone is narrow, so the small debit is lost in full most of the time; with three strikes and four contracts, transaction costs consume a large share of the theoretical edge, and short-gamma whipsaw near the body strike close to expiration is severe.
concept.misconceptions: A butterfly's high reward-to-risk ratio is not free money — the maximum payoff is attained only at one exact price, so probability-weighted value, not the peak, determines fairness.
concept.example: Buy the $95 call, sell two $100 calls, buy the $105 call for a $1.00 net debit. Max value $5.00 at $100 (gain $4.00); outside $95-$105 the $100 debit is lost; breakevens at $96 and $104.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
